content: A search through more than 60,000 bone fragments uncovered the first confirmed Denisovan radius, a forearm bone offering rare clues to how these ancient human relatives were built. A forearm fragment from a cave in southwest China combines features resembling those of Neanderthals and modern humans, yet it belonged to neither. Proteins preserved in the bone identify its owner as Denisovan, part of an ancient human group recognized through genetic evidence. The fragment is the first, and so far only, confirmed Denisovan radius, one of the two long bones in the forearm. Denisovans are thought to have lived across much of Asia, but their fossil record is sparse, particularly for bones below the skull. That scarcity has left researchers with little evidence of the physical traits that helped them adapt to different environments. The radius is among five remains from Bianfu Cave in Yunnan Province that a new study identified as Denisovan. Dating to the late Middle Pleistocene, the fossils fill a longstanding gap in the group’s known distribution in southwest China. Professor Qiaomei Fu of the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology (IVPP) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) led the research in collaboration with multiple institutions. The findings were published in Nature on September 9. Cataloged as BFD771, the radius fragment preserves the end nearest the elbow. Its large dimensions at that end resemble Neanderthal radii, as does the likely inward orientation of its radial tuberosity, the bony projection where the biceps muscle attaches. Its overall external shape, however, is closer to that of modern humans. So is the geometry of a cross section through the middle of its neck, the narrowed region near the elbow end. The researchers interpret this combination as evidence of distinctive mechanical demands and behavioral adaptations in Denisovans, differing from those inferred for Neanderthals and modern humans. Two skull fragments, BFD767 and BFD769, provided another anatomical comparison. Both are pieces of parietal bones, which form part of the top and sides of the skull. Their skull vault thickness patterns most closely resemble those of Homo heidelbergensis and late Middle Pleistocene archaic Homo from East Asia. Finding these bones required narrowing a collection of more than 60,000 fragments. Researchers increasingly use Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry, or ZooMS, to screen large fossil collections by examining protein signatures. The technique requires minimally invasive sampling and is simple, fast, and relatively inexpensive. Even so, hominin fossil recovery rates at sites such as Denisova Cave and Baishiya Karst Cave have been just 0.1%. Applying ZooMS to every fragment from Bianfu Cave would have been costly and inefficient. The team instead developed a “morphological pre-screening + ZooMS identification” strategy, first examining bone shapes to select 22 potential hominin remains. ZooMS then confirmed that the two parietal fragments and the radius fragment belonged to hominins, the group that includes humans and our extinct close relatives. The combined approach substantially improved screening efficiency and provides a repeatable method for searching other Paleolithic sites with abundant bone fragments. BFD767 and BFD771 came from Layer 7, dated to approximately 148,000 to 134,000 years ago. That layer also contained four hominin teeth, two of which the researchers included in the study: a lower fourth premolar, YHB3518, and a lower second molar, YHB3075. The other skull fragment, BFD769, came from the older Layer 9, dated to approximately 167,000 to 150,000 years ago. Identifying the bones as hominin remains did not reveal which ancient human group they belonged to. To find out, researchers analyzed proteins preserved in three bones and two teeth, recovering 6 to 16 proteins from each specimen. Protein fragments in the tooth enamel also indicated that both teeth belonged to males. All five fossils carried the Denisovan-specific protein variant COL1A2 R996K. Additional variants in the teeth supported this identification and helped distinguish the fossils from other ancient human groups, including Homo erectus . The researchers also constructed evolutionary trees using the recovered protein sequences. All five specimens clustered with the Denisovan specimen Denisova 3, with 100% posterior probability, providing strong support for their identification. These findings make Bianfu Cave the richest known source of Denisovan fossils outside Denisova Cave. Dating to a glacial period known as Marine Isotope Stage 6, the remains suggest that the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau’s relatively warm climate and abundant food resources may have provided a favorable habitat for Denisovans. Reference: “Ancient proteins identify various Denisovan remains from Southwest China” by Huiyun Rao, Song Xing, Qijun Ruan, Fan Bai, Yuhao Zhao, Zhongyou Wu, Siyuan Tang, E. Andrew Bennett, Xiaotian Feng, Sungui Lin, Qingfeng Shao, Xiong Yang, Zitao Li, Kai Zhou, Feng Liu and Qiaomei Fu, 9 September 2026, Nature . title: SK Hynix third-quarter profit sharply beats estimates on AI memory boost
content: South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix on Wednesday released its third-quarter earnings results, posting a record high quarterly profit that sharply beats estimates, while announcing over $25 billion in dividends and buybacks. Here are SK Hynix's third-quarter results compared with LSEG SmartEstimates, which are weighted toward forecasts from analysts who are more consistently accurate: Revenue rose 327.9% from a year earlier, while operating profit climbed 632.1% year on year. Compared with the previous quarter, revenue climbed 31.9%, while operating profit surged 37.6%. SK Hynix posted record quarterly revenue and operating profit, with sales exceeding 100 trillion won for the first time, as it announced plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders — including at least 30 trillion won in cash dividends and 60 trillion won in share buybacks and cancellations. The chipmaker approved a third-quarter dividend of 14 trillion won, including a special dividend funded by gains from its investment in Kioxia. The company will also buyback 20 trillion won in shares, half of which will be cancelled this year. SK Hynix expects HBM4 to surpass HBM3E in both shipments and revenue in the fourth quarter, as it ramps up production at its M15X facility in Cheongju, South Korea. HBM, or high-bandwidth memory, is a type of advanced memory used alongside AI processors to handle large amounts of data. HBM4 is the sixth generation of the technology. The company has secured long-term agreements with 14 major customers covering more than 50% of its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. It expects memory demand to outpace supply through 2030 and plans to significantly increase investment next year. In August, SK Hynix had announced plans to repurchase and cancel 40 trillion won worth of its own shares, while raising its shareholder return target to more than 50% of cumulative free cash flow generated between 2025 and 2027. Last week, SK Hynix announced that its U.S. subsidiary Solidigm would halt its review of potential pre-IPO fundraising and IPO options, citing market volatility and share price trends. The company said it would continue to assess investment timing, scale and financing options to support Solidigm's growth and enhance shareholder value.

title: Chart: Anthropic's cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company
content: Anthropic has more cash than almost every company in America. The nearly 6-year-old artificial intelligence lab disclosed on Monday in an S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it had $112.4 billion in cash, plus another $19.3 billion in short-term investments, as of June 30. Anthropic's total of $131.7 billion surpasses every non-bank U.S. company, except for Berkshire Hathaway and Alphabet , according to data compiled by CNBC and S&P Capital IQ. As of midyear, Anthropic had more cash than Amazon , SpaceX , Meta and Microsoft . It had more than Nvidia and Apple combined. Depending on how much the company raises in its initial public offering — and reports suggest it could top $100 billion — Anthropic could bump its hoard to more than $230 billion in cash. So far, Anthropic hasn't shared specific details about its offering size, and it said in the filing that existing investors would also be selling into the IPO – meaning the company itself won't collect the entire fundraise. Those details are expected to be disclosed in about two weeks. Never before has a company gone public with anywhere near this amount of cash. Anthropic's trove underscores the fundraising prowess that has allowed it to amass an aggregate of $141 billion in private financing in just six years since its founding. However, given the company's future commitments for computing power that have yet to hit its expenses, Anthropic will have to continue accumulating cash through fundraising or generating profits to fulfill its obligations. Anthropic's first-half compute and infrastructure expenses totaled $8.95 billion. But the company said it usually buys computing power 12 to 18 months ahead of time, and only recognizes expenses as that capacity becomes available. That means the first-half expense figure doesn't capture the full scale of its future obligations. As of June 30, Anthropic disclosed $321.4 billion in estimated future undiscounted lease obligations and $265.6 billion in expected future fixed or minimum-guaranteed commitments — more than half a trillion total. These will commence within the next few years, with terms ranging from one year to 20 years. Additionally, the company said that subsequent to June 30, it entered into new and amended agreements with a minimum future payment obligation of about $245 billion. The company hasn't shared an aggregate amount of its up-to-date commitments yet. If Anthropic's cash is king, compute is its biggest claim on the crown. —CNBC's Ritika Shah and Nick Wells contributed to this article.
